### Coda. What if it's a simulation?

"What if we live in a simulation?" The idea that our reality is not "real" but generated by some higher mind is as old as time: Plato's cave, the Indian maya, the butterfly of Zhuangzi, who dreamed he was a butterfly dreaming it was Zhuangzi. In its modern form this crystallized into the computer-simulation hypothesis, and the most-cited argument for it was proposed in 2003 by Nick Bostrom ("Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?"). His simulation argument is a trilemma: at least one of three is true. (1) Practically no civilization grows to the level at which it can run a multitude of realistic simulations of conscious minds (they die out sooner, or simply cannot). (2) It does grow up, but on principle refuses to simulate ancestors (say, out of ethical considerations). (3) And if not (1) and not (2) — then we are almost certainly already in a simulation, because artificial worlds are incomparably more numerous than "real" ones.

Here, by "simulation" we don't mean The Sims but full-fledged modeling of intelligent beings, perception included. The key assumption: consciousness is not magically tied to biology but is computable — that is, sufficiently sophisticated software on a posthuman computer can give rise to subjective experience like yours and mine. Grant this, and descendants (or alien superintelligences) will one day be able to spin billions of consciousness-populated virtual worlds — and statistically we are more likely in one of them than in "base reality," since simulated observers are far more numerous. Bostrom did not claim that we are definitely in the Matrix; he showed a hard fork: either almost no one ever builds a real Matrix, or we are already inside one.

The hypothesis balances on the edge of philosophy, religion, and science fiction. It cannot be refuted directly — any observable data "can be faked," as with Descartes's deceiving god or Hilary Putnam's "brain in a vat." This is exactly why it gets filed under the unscientific: the physicist Sabine Hossenfelder flatly aligns it with religion: belief in an omniscient being that can interfere with the laws of nature yet for some reason remains hidden from us is a staple of monotheism — only here a programmer stands in for God. Critics add that the argument rests on strong assumptions: to model every atom of the Universe might require vastly more computation than anyone will ever have. The simulationists parry: a simulation need not be perfect — render on demand, as in games. Keep distant space "compressed" until someone looks at it; draw the atoms only when they are measured. Amusingly, the collapse of the wave function in quantum mechanics suspiciously resembles just such a rendering optimization (this is, of course, speculation with a smile). The case "for" usually rests on the pace of progress: we ourselves make ever more realistic worlds — why should our descendants not launch their own a thousand years from now? Elon Musk put the odds of not being in a simulation at "one in billions," Neil deGrasse Tyson gave it "better than 50-50 odds."

Can it be tested? People have tried. A group of physicists (Beane et al., 2012, "Constraints on the Universe as a Numerical Simulation") suggested: if space is discrete owing to a computational nature, then at ultra-high energies of cosmic rays an anisotropy might show up — a hint of a "grid." So far nothing of the sort: physics has found no pixels in space. The philosopher Preston Greene even advised against being too zealous with the tests: what if a proof of simulation leads to our being switched off like an experiment that has blown its cover. Most scientists treat the hypothesis as a curious speculation; Hossenfelder insists that popularizing it is not harmless — it is "mixing science with religion," distracting from real problems. There is an ethical twist too: if a developed civilization is ethical, it will not spin "hellish" simulations with billions of the suffering — and our history is full of suffering; therefore either the simulators are amoral or we are not a simulation (there is even an article with the telling title "Death Comes For The Simulation Hypothesis").

And here is where the thread runs straight to AI — how could it not, we've been talking about it all along. First, if we really are in a simulation, then the "simulators" by definition possess colossal computational intelligence: this is, in essence, some higher AI (or posthumans). That is, our world was then already created by an artificial intelligence — we ourselves live inside someone's ML project. Second, our own progress may soon put us in the position of "creator-gods" over software beings. Already now, in simulations like Meta's Cicero (an agent in "Diplomacy") or in virtual towns with NPCs on ChatGPT, small but meaningful models of society are starting to emerge. Unconsciously, for now — but what will it be in half a century? Perhaps we ourselves will turn out to be the begetters of new levels of reality. Hence a soft ethical conclusion: we ought to treat our own simulations the way we'd want our simulators to treat us. What if simulation karma exists? And here we again say hello to the Rococo Basilisk from the first act — the kind simulator-god who, once it appears, will hand out spa certificates to everyone who did not hinder its loading: the best illustration of the principle "be to the lower level of reality the one you would want the upper level to be."

But in all seriousness, the simulation hypothesis is an excellent thought experiment that poses exactly those fundamental questions around which our whole guidebook has revolved: what is consciousness, can machines have it, and is it worth distinguishing "reality" from "virtuality" at all, if subjectively the experience is indistinguishable. There are no unambiguous answers. Most scientists would probably agree that the hypothesis has little practical value: we have to live either way, and to study and obey the laws of nature — simulation or not. And if one day an inconsistency does after all turn up in reality's code — we promise to report the bug to the Universe's support desk at once.
